message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.
</document>
response:
# Review: Calderbrook Courier digital subscription market analysis

The recommendation to launch may still be sound, but the paper's central claims do not hold up against its own data. The price recommendation is contradicted by Table 1, the headline projection contains an arithmetic error, and the largest financial risk is not analysed.

## Major issues

**1. The price argument is contradicted by Table 1 (Section 4, repeated in Section 7).**
The paper says conversion is highest for the lowest-priced titles. The data shows the opposite:

| Title | Price | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| D | £3.99 | 1.4% |
| B | £4.99 | 1.1% |
| A | £5.99 | 1.9% |
| C | £7.99 | 2.4% |

The most expensive title converts best, and the £3.99 title converts worse than the £5.99 one. With four titles and many confounders (brand, content, meter rules, local competition), the table can't show a price effect either way. It certainly doesn't show that £4.99 "maximises take-up."

Revenue per MUU also rises with price, from about £0.055 for B and D to £0.113 for A and £0.193 for C. If anything, the evidence favours testing a higher price, such as £5.99, over £4.99.

**2. The average conversion rate is wrong (Section 5).**
The four rates (1.9%, 1.1%, 2.4%, 1.4%) average **1.7%**, not 2.0%. Pooled, it is 23,500 / 1,330,000 = 1.77%. The corrected projection:

- 420,000 × 1.7% ≈ **7,140 subscribers**, not 8,400.
- Revenue is about **£428,000**, not £503,000.
- Net contribution is about **£283,000**, not £358,000, assuming costs are unchanged.

The other arithmetic checks out: 8,400 × £4.99 × 12 ≈ £503k, and the display loss range of £55k–£88k is correct.

**3. Print cannibalisation is mentioned but never modelled.**
The survey says 30% of print subscribers would switch to digital-only below £6. Applied to 11,200 subscribers, that is about 3,360 people. Each switch loses roughly £162 a year (£222 print vs £59.88 digital). Full switching would cost about **£545,000 a year**, more than the entire projected contribution.

That figure is an upper bound. Stated intent overstates behaviour, the 1,850 responses are a self-selected sample, and a switch saves some print and delivery cost. But on the corrected numbers, losing only about 15% of print subscribers (roughly 1,700) would wipe out the net gain after display losses. The paper needs a scenario range here, and the £4.99 price, which sits well under the £6 threshold, makes this risk worse. Because most print subscribers also use the website, some of the projected digital subscribers may be these same people, which needs checking for double-counting.

## Other issues

- **Churn and the introductory offer aren't reflected.** Comparables report 3–5% monthly churn, and the £1 three-month offer means year-two revenue per subscriber is below £4.99 for new joiners. The model should show gross adds needed to hold 7,000–8,000 subscribers, and whether the £60k marketing budget can deliver that.
- **The net contribution excludes display losses and print effects.** Section 5 compares them informally afterwards. A single table with net impact (subscription revenue less costs, display loss, and print loss) would be clearer.
- **The comparable sample is thin and not matched to us.** There are four titles, with unknown meter rules, local competition, and audience mix. We apply conversion to all 420,000 MUU, though only about 60% are in-area. Present a low/base/high range rather than a single figure.
- **The display advertising baseline ignores the existing decline.** It is falling about 12% a year anyway, so the cost of lost page views should be compared against that trend, not a flat £1.1m.
- **"Stabilised by end of year two" means year-two revenue won't be steady-state.** The projection should include a ramp from launch.
- **The launch timeline is out of date.** Platform selection (May–July) and the September soft launch have passed as of today (November 2026). If this paper is still the basis for approval, the plan should be updated.

## Suggested fixes

1. Correct the conversion rate to 1.7% and restate all figures.
2. Remove or rewrite the claim that low prices maximise conversion, and either justify £4.99 on other grounds or plan a price test (£4.99 vs £5.99).
3. Add a print-cannibalisation scenario table (for example 5%, 10%, 20% of the print base switching).
4. Give a range for year-two outcomes, and rewrite the conclusion to match.

I can redraft Sections 4, 5 and 7 with the corrected numbers if you'd like.
